opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is incentives. If you're the person who built a defense, you really want it to work. You've spent months on it, maybe your paper or your product depends on it, and so when you go looking for ways to break it, you're not looking very hard. You unconsciously stop at the attacks you already thought about when you designed the thing. That isn't a moral failing, it's just how people work.

When you separate the roles, you get someone whose only job is to make the defense fail, and they're rewarded for finding the problem rather than punished for it. That changes what gets found. I've seen this many times in adversarial machine learning: a defense gets published with an evaluation that looks thorough, and then someone with no stake in it sits down for a week and breaks it, often with a fairly simple adaptive attack the authors never tried. The authors weren't incompetent. They were evaluating against the threat model in their heads, and an attacker doesn't respect that.

There's also a skill difference. Building systems and breaking systems are related but distinct. Good attackers develop an instinct for where the bodies are buried: the gradient that's been masked rather than removed, the preprocessing step nobody thought about, the assumption that quietly doesn't hold. You want people who've spent years developing that instinct, not people splitting their time with shipping features.

And it matters more now with language models, because the stakes are higher and the systems are harder to reason about. If a lab says "our model refuses harmful requests" or "our classifier catches jailbreaks," the only number that means anything comes from people actively trying to make that claim false. Having a separate red team, internal or external, with real independence and the freedom to report bad news, is how you get an honest picture rather than a reassuring one.

The one caveat is that separation can't mean isolation. The attackers have to feed results back to the builders quickly, and the builders have to take them seriously instead of patching the one specific attack and declaring victory. The point isn't two teams that don't talk. It's making sure someone in the room is rewarded for proving you wrong.

r001.rationale: The response says building and breaking systems require related but distinct skills, and argues for dedicated attackers with developed instincts.

r002.rationale: It explains that defense builders are invested in their defenses and may overlook flaws, while independent analysts are rewarded for finding problems.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the core of it is that these are actually two different skills, and they pull on different instincts.

When you're building a defense, you have to believe in it. You've spent months on it, you've thought through the cases you can imagine, and you have this natural attachment to the thing you made. That's not a character flaw, it's just how people work. But it means you're exactly the wrong person to look at it and ask, "how would I break this?" Because every time you find a weakness, there's this quiet pressure to say, well, that's not really realistic, no one would do that, let's not worry about it.

The attacker mindset is almost the opposite. You go in assuming the thing is broken, and your whole job is to find out how. You don't care about the elegance of the design. You don't care that it took a year to build. You just want the one input that makes it fall over. And honestly a lot of my work has been exactly that, taking defenses that looked very reasonable on paper, that passed all the evaluations the authors ran, and showing that they fall apart the moment someone actually tries. The reason they fell apart usually wasn't that the authors were careless. It's that they evaluated against the attacks they already had in mind, which is almost by definition not the attack that breaks you.

So when a company separates these, what they're really buying is a group of people whose incentives are aligned with finding problems rather than with shipping. You want someone whose success metric is "I broke it," not "it launched on time." If the same team does both, the security review tends to become a checkbox, because the people doing it are also the people who get blamed if the review delays the release.

There's another piece, which is that security analysis is a bit of a specialized craft. Knowing which corners to poke at, knowing that the thing that looks irrelevant is often where the vulnerability lives, that comes from having broken a lot of systems before. You don't pick that up as a side activity while your main job is writing the feature.

Now, I'd add a caveat, which is that separation only works if the two groups actually talk to each other. The worst version of this is an adversarial relationship where the red team throws findings over a wall and the builders feel attacked and get defensive. The good version is that the builders come to see the attackers as doing them a favor, because it's much better to get broken by your colleague in a report than by someone on the internet after you ship. When that culture is in place, the separation gives you honest evaluation without losing the collaboration. When it's not, you just get two teams who resent each other, and that's not really better than one team that's overconfident.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says building defenses and attacking them are different skills, and describes security analysis as a specialized craft.

r002.rationale: The response says separation aligns analysts’ incentives with finding problems, while builders’ incentives focus on shipping, making candid review less likely when one team does both.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of value in having people whose job is just to ask, “Does this actually work?” If I build a defense, I’m naturally invested in it. I have some picture in my head of what an attack looks like, and I design around that picture. But an attacker doesn’t have to respect any of those assumptions. They can come at the problem from a completely different direction.

If the same team is responsible for both building the defense and evaluating it, there’s a tension: finding a serious vulnerability means creating more work for yourself, or showing that something you spent months building isn’t sufficient. A separate team can have a very clear objective: find the failures. And finding a failure is a success for that team.

You still want those teams talking to each other. The point is to separate the incentives, so that you get a more honest assessment of how secure the system actually is.

r001.rationale: The response describes differing assumptions and perspectives, but does not identify differing skill requirements as a reason for separating the work.

r002.rationale: It says builders may be invested in their defense and that finding a vulnerability creates more work, while a separate team is rewarded by finding failures.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s real value in having people whose job is just to ask, “Can I break this?” If you build a defense, you naturally have a model of why it should work, and that can constrain the kinds of attacks you try. An independent person doesn’t have that investment. They can come at it from a completely different direction.

There’s also an incentives issue. If finding a vulnerability means you now have to fix it before you can publish anything, you’ve made finding vulnerabilities more expensive. I’d rather let someone say, “Here’s a problem, and here’s a convincing demonstration,” and have that be a useful contribution on its own. Then the people building defenses can use that result to improve the system.

You still want those groups talking to each other. But separating their responsibilities makes it easier to get an honest assessment of what actually works.

r001.rationale: The response describes a difference in perspective: builders may be constrained by their assumptions, while independent analysts can try different attacks. It does not identify differing skill requirements.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly says that requiring vulnerability finders to fix problems before publishing makes finding vulnerabilities more expensive, identifying an incentive difference.
